text: No new theory in this lesson — four fully worked problems that put the last four lessons' tools to work end to end: find the eigenvalues, find the eigenvectors, diagonalize, and verify every step numerically.

Problem one: for A equals 4,2,1,3, the characteristic equation works out to lambda squared minus 7 lambda plus 10 equals zero, factoring to lambda equals 5 or lambda equals 2. Solving gives the eigenvectors 2,1 for lambda 5, and 1, negative 1 for lambda 2 — both confirmed by multiplying back through A v equals lambda v.

Problem two: diagonalizing that same matrix builds P from those eigenvectors and D from the eigenvalues, 5 and 2, on the diagonal. Inverting P and multiplying P, D, and P inverse back together reconstructs exactly 4,2,1,3 — the original matrix A.

Problem three: the Pauli-X gate, 0,1,1,0, has the exact same eigenvalues as Pauli-Z, plus one and minus one — but completely different eigenvectors, 1,1 and 1, negative 1. Those are exactly proportional to the states called ket-plus and ket-minus — Pauli-X's eigenvectors are a different, 'diagonal' basis from Pauli-Z's.

Problem four diagonalizes Pauli-X the same way, building P and D from its eigenvectors and eigenvalues, inverting P, and multiplying everything back together to reconstruct X exactly. Across all four problems, every claimed result got checked by multiplying back out — that habit, not the algebra itself, is what actually catches wrong answers.
Chapter 5 picks up from here with the full complex generalization of length and angle: inner products, and the Hilbert space idea that sits underneath everything you've learned so far.
